confirmed: The full markdown was read through its end, including all appendices and embedded example papers; the PDF has 131 pages and is stamped arXiv:2506.20803v1 [cs.CL], 25 Jun 2025, matching source.version (PDF p. 1; document page count; final PDF p. 131).
The title and authors match: The Ideation–Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas; Chenglei Si, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Diyi Yang (PDF p. 1).

People were individually randomized to execute an anonymized LLM-generated or human-expert idea from preferred topics, with blinded expert review of their resulting projects. The supplied-ideas intervention supports has_randomized_people_study=true, field_rct, ideas_supplied, and ai_vs_active (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 2.1-2.2).

The execution sample contains 43 analyzed people, one project per person: 19 human-idea executors and 24 AI-idea executors. The 66 count is onboarded participants; the paper does not unambiguously give the full pre-attrition randomized total or arm allocation. Keep n_randomized=null, core=no, criterion_2=not_met, and context_class=none (PDF p. 3, Section 2.1 and Table 1; p. 5, Section 3.1 and Table 2).

One assigned project was terminated because the idea was too vague and infeasible; other noncompletion was attributed to personal reasons. The form's 23 noncompleters is the arithmetic difference between 66 onboarded and 43 completed, not a separately printed randomized count (PDF p. 4, Section 2.2; p. 5, Section 3.1).

The AI ideation agent was based on Claude-3.5-Sonnet; projects spanned 7 NLP topics. Researchers came from the US, Australia, India, the UK, Nepal, Singapore, and Canada; mean prior paper counts were 15.3 in the human arm and 14.3 in the AI arm (PDF p. 3, Introduction continuation and Table 1; p. 5, Table 2 and Sections 3.1-3.2).
There were 58 expert reviewers and 181 reviews, not 181 execution participants; Table 3 comprises 85 human-condition and 96 AI-condition reviews (PDF p. 5, Section 3.1; p. 6, Table 3).

Table 4 execution means and two-sided FDR p-values match all three reported strings: overall Human 3.968 versus AI 3.406, p=0.175; novelty 4.903 versus 4.729, p=0.586; effectiveness 4.782 versus 4.125, p=0.266 (PDF p. 7, Table 4).

Table 5 gaps and FDR p-values match: overall Human -0.628 versus AI -1.976, Human-minus-AI 1.348, p=0.004**; novelty -0.010 versus -1.049, difference 1.039, p=0.025*; effectiveness -0.052 versus -1.879, difference 1.827, p=0.003**. These are raw score changes on the rating scale, not standardized effect sizes (PDF p. 7, Table 5 and Section 4.2).

Table 3 review-level numbers match: overall Human 4.00 (SD 1.59) versus AI 3.41 (SD 1.46), p=0.01*; novelty 4.93 (SD 1.61) versus 4.73 (SD 1.75), p=0.21; effectiveness 4.84 (SD 2.11) versus 4.12 (SD 1.94), p=0.01*. All of these p-values are one-sided and FDR-adjusted (PDF p. 6, Table 3 and caption).
The one-line finding correctly distinguishes the larger AI ideation-execution score drops from nonsignificant project-level execution-score comparisons (PDF p. 7, Tables 4-5; p. 6, Section 4.1).

The included appendices contain the review rubric, institution tables, score plots, ideation-execution correlations, sensitivity analysis excluding 6 AI ideas, metric correlations, and example projects. This is an original execution experiment, not a synthesis; no pooled-study estimates are reported (PDF pp. 18-30, Appendices A-G; pp. 31-131, Appendix H).
summary: The arXiv v1 reports a randomized field experiment with 43 analyzed people, warranting two-screener review but falling below the 50-person core threshold. Recorded estimates and the one-line finding match the PDF; corrections address outcome coding and omissions, statistical metadata, preregistration, effort wording, provenance, funding, and data availability.
